paras: The pursuit of Shep Johnson took place on the morning of August 17, 1910, at Thirteenth and C streets southwest in Washington, D.C., when a crowd chased and surrounded a Black man carrying fish in the belief that he had just shot someone. The shot had in fact been fired by William Javins, who had tried to kill himself, and a policeman who saw it cleared Johnson before he was harmed. The Washington Times headlined the incident as a threatened lynching.

About 10:30 a.m., Javins, a twenty-six-year-old ice cream delivery worker, put a revolver in his mouth and fired after delivering to a store at 1300 C street. According to the Times, Johnson was walking up C street with a string of fish from the fish wharf and was not five feet away when the shot went off. The paper said, in a joking passage, that he feared a game warden had fired at him for fishing in the closed season, dropped his fish and ran.

Bystanders took off after him, and someone yelled, "There he goes; he did it." The Evening Star wrote that the pursuing party grew as the chase went on, with cries of "Murder" and "Catch him," until Johnson was almost exhausted and forced to stop. The crowd hemmed him in, and the Times wrote that "it looked as if the negro would be handled pretty roughly."

Policeman Bartemann of the Fourth precinct, who had seen the shooting and tried to stop Javins, then told the crowd that Johnson had nothing to do with it. Johnson gathered up what was left of his fish and left, and no injury to him is reported.
Javins was taken to Emergency Hospital, where the bullet was removed and he was expected to recover. No report of any arrest of members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The incident was reported in Washington's white dailies, and of these only the Times and the Star described the chase. The Times put "Lynching Threatened in Southwest When Shot Is Fired" in its headline and called Johnson innocent, yet told the chase as comedy, with slang such as "hit the grit" and a dialect plea beginning "Deed, boss." The Star, under the headline "Another Flees Madly," called him "Seth Johnson, a veteran fish dealer" and did not give his race.
The Washington Herald's next-day story covered only the suicide attempt and left out the chase.

reader.title: Pursuit of Shep Johnson
bases: A crowd chased and surrounded a Black man it believed had done a shooting and, per the headline, threatened lynching, but no blow or injury is reported before a policeman cleared him (A1, A2).

The Washington Times and the Evening Star independently report the same-day crowd chase of a fish-carrying Johnson after Javins shot himself, though they differ on his first name and only the Times gives his race (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Washington Times reporter
accounts.gist: Johnson, fearing a game warden had fired at him for fishing out of season, ran; the crowd chased and hemmed him in on a shout that he did it, and 'it looked as if the negro would be handled pretty roughly' until Policeman Bartemann cleared him.

accounts.label: Evening Star reporter
accounts.gist: Seth Johnson, alarmed by the report, ran toward the river; pedestrians assumed he had done the shooting, and a growing party crying 'Murder' and 'Catch him' pursued him until he was almost exhausted and forced to stop.

framing.detail: The Times headlined 'Lynching Threatened' and called Johnson innocent, but told the chase as comedy, with 'hit the grit' and a dialect plea ('Deed, boss').
The Star folded the chase into its suicide story under 'Another Flees Madly' and named no race.
The Herald reported only the suicide attempt and left out the chase.

record_check.dossier: The crowd believed Johnson had fired the shot that wounded William Javins (a suicide attempt); the game-warden fear was, per the Times, Johnson's own reason for running, not a shot at him.
Black ('negro') per the Times; the Star gives no race.
Pursuit and surrounding by the crowd; no violence reported.
Unnamed bystanders and pedestrians, a crowd that grew during the chase.
The Times headline says 'Lynching Threatened'; the body says only that he might have been 'handled pretty roughly'.
Two Washington papers reported the chase (Times, Star); a third (Herald) reported only the suicide attempt.

info: Thirteenth and C streets southwest, Washington, D.C., outside a store at 1300 C street
"Shep" Johnson (Times), described as a negro carrying a string of fish; the Star calls him "Seth Johnson, a veteran fish dealer" and gives no race
Bystanders took it that he had fired the shot; someone yelled "There he goes; he did it" and the Star reports cries of "Murder". The shot was in fact William Javins's attempt to kill himself.
Persons in the neighborhood and pedestrians who heard the shot; no names given
Bartemann told the crowd Johnson had no hand in the shooting; Johnson picked up his fish and left
